# The Quiet Power of Noticing

I've been thinking about attention lately—how it's become our most precious commodity, constantly fragmented across notifications and demands. But there's something profound in simply noticing things.

This morning, I watched sunlight move across my desk. Not while doing anything else—just watching. The way it caught dust particles, turned them golden, made the ordinary visible. It took maybe two minutes, but it felt substantial in a way my usual rushing around doesn't.

We're taught to optimize everything, to extract maximum productivity from each moment. But I wonder if we've lost something in that equation. The mathematician Euler apparently solved problems while holding his baby. Not in spite of the distraction, but perhaps because his mind was free to wander while his hands were occupied.

There's a myth that depth requires isolation, that meaningful work demands intense focus sessions scheduled like meetings. But I think depth also lives in the margins—in noticing how a conversation made you feel, in remembering why you cared about something in the first place, in the small observations that remind you why you're doing anything at all.

Maybe the antidote to fragmentation isn't more discipline but more gentleness with ourselves. Not another productivity system, but permission to notice things without immediately turning them into content or lessons.

The sunlight moved on. I returned to work. But something shifted, small and unmeasurable. I was more present for the next task, more aware of what mattered about it.

That feels like enough.
